newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai phone operators seen facing difficulties.
newsitem.headline: New Thai phone operators seen facing difficulties.

text.p: New mobile phone operators hoping to crack Thailand's market will face an uphill task competing with existing operators armed with established national coverage and large customer bases, analysts said on Sunday.

Last week, Thailand's deputy transport and communication minister Direk Charoenpol said his ministry would this month seek cabinet approval for its proposal to allow new mobile telephone operators to enter the market.
He said the government planned to grant between four and five new mobile phone operator licences to private companies.
The move was aimed at further liberalising the local mobile phone and telecommunications industry, he added.

The announcement sparked a sell-off in telecommunication shares, especially mobile phone stocks, as investors anticipated lower earnings by existing companies once new entrants were allowed into the market.
But analysts said worries about the threat posed by new operators to existing ones were exaggerated because it would take at least two years for new entrants to build a nationwide network.

"It's very difficult for those new guys to break into the market. The coverage is not going to be from day one, equal to, or better coverage than existing operators," Michael Millar, research manager at SocGen-Crosby Securities, told Reuters.
"The market is very coverage conscious. So new guys have to come in from day one with similar or better coverage," he said.
Currently two private mobile phone operators -- Advanced Info Services Plc and Total Access Communication Plc -- control Thailand's mobile phone business.
A third operator, Wireless Communications Service, a joint venture between International Engineering Plc and Total Access, is expected to begin providing mobile phone services later this year.
Analysts said another factor new operators would have to face would be the sluggish economy that could weaken overall demand for new mobile phones.
"The Thai economy is going to slow down and that may affect the number of new subscribers," said Paul Ngo, an investment analyst at ING Barings.
Thailand officially expects the national economy to grow by 6.8 percent this year. The growth rate dropped below double digits after nearly a decade to 6.7 percent in 1996.

But some private analysts see growth sinking under six percent this year as weak exports, slowing private and manufacturing activity as well as turmoil in the financial and property sectors take their toll on the economy.
Ngo at Barings said consumers would be the major beneficiaries when new operators enter the market as service airtime charges and handset prices would drop as the number of providers increased.
